newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Flynn urges wider EU rules on worker consultation.
newsitem.headline: Flynn urges wider EU rules on worker consultation.

text.p: Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn called on Wednesday for European Union rules which would oblige companies in the EU to set up systems at national level for consulting their workers on major decisions.

He added that these rules should contain sanctions on firms that failed to consult their employees properly and in good time on decisions that affect their jobs, including the possibility of annulling the decision itself.

"Community action is necessary," Flynn told a news conference to announce the publication of a European Commission consultation paper which asks trades unions and employers to say within six weeks whether they think there is a need for general EU rules on consulting workers at national level.

The EU had general rules obliging large multinational companies to consult their workers, and more patchy rules requiring national companies to consult employees on several specific issues, such as imminent collective redundancies and transfers of enterprises, but these rules were "not perfect (and) not complete", Flynn said.
Different member states have different rules and Ireland and Britain have no national consultation provisions at all.
Common rules would eliminate distortions of competition and ensure equal treatment for workers throughout the EU, the Commission's consultation paper argues.

Tougher sanctions might also help to stop firms breaching the rules, Flynn said, adding that recent violations had "considerably undermined" public confidence in a European Union with a human, social face.

The Commission's initiative, which Flynn has been advocating for several years, comes in the wake of a much-criticised decision by car maker Renault to close its assembly plant in Vilvoorde, Belgium, with the loss of 3,100 jobs.
"We need to look at a better way of enforcement of information and consultation...notably by nullifying decisions made in violation of the relevant rules," Flynn said.
EU governments rejected this idea when the Commission first proposed it in 1991 but Flynn said he hoped they would now have a rethink.
Renault would have been forced to reverse its decision, which has been suspended but not revoked by the Belgian and French courts, if member states had agreed to the 1991 proposal, he stressed.
The commissioner said new EU rules were also needed because some firms did not inform or consult their workers properly.
"We would like to see the consultations and the information in sufficient time so that alternatives can be considered with a view to preventing the loss of jobs," he said.

"These discussions... can't just be confined only to the social aspects of the management decisions. I would be much happier if they also included economic and the strategic issues that are behind all of these decisions," he continued.

When the Commission published a discussion paper on worker information and consultation in November 1995, the European employers group UNICE said it disliked the idea of an EU-level framework agreement.

Flynn said he hoped they would now accept that apart from the fact that workers had a "fundamental right" to be consulted, doing so was good for business because it helped get the best out of employees and boost productivity.

If representatives of unions and employers -- the so-called social partners -- decide that EU level action is necessary, they will have nine months to negotiate an agreement based on more specific Commission proposals.
